article.title: Why are Mexican cartels fighting in Ukraine?
article.author: Zoe Alexandra
article.content: The war in Ukraine has become a training ground for Latin America’s drug cartels: An enforcer for one of Brazil’s biggest gangs was arrested in Rio this month after five on the front lines in Europe. Peter Korotaev, independent journalist and author of Events in Ukraine, joins Zoe Alexandra to unpack why Colombian ex-soldiers, Mexican cartel members and members of a Pentecostal Brazilian gang wound up among the foreign mercenaries fighting Russian forces. Some serve in units tied to HUR, Ukraine’s CIA-trained military intelligence agency, and to the far-right Azov movement, whose longtime leader Serhiy Korotkikh openly follows narco folk saint Santa Muerte. And as cartel drone attacks surge from Mexico to Brazil, Korotaev argues, the violence gives Washington the pretext it needs for further US military intervention in Latin America. Inside Ukraine, Korotaev lays out a forced conscription crisis that has turned the public against Zelensky’s draft, from street roundups by recruitment officers to an Azov detention site outside Kyiv, where soldiers were allegedly beaten and protesters who gathered outside arrested. He breaks down the corruption scandal tying top Ukrainian law enforcement officials to a multibillion-dollar scam call center industry, one he says the European press keeps buried to protect Zelensky. And he explains why Europe, not Moscow or Washington, may be the biggest obstacle to a peace deal in Abu Dhabi. Cartel recruits, CIA-trained spies and a NATO-backed war machine built on systemic corruption: This is the Ukraine story the corporate media won’t report. Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! ****** Rough transcript follows: [Host:] It has been more than four and a half years since the start of the war in Ukraine, and there are strong signs that diplomacy is starting up again. Earlier this month, Russian and Ukrainian negotiators met face to face in Abu Dhabi for the first time in nine months, with the United States mediating. Yet, as we’ve seen in the past week, attacks have continued in Ukrainian and Russian territory. Today, Russian President Vladimir Putin is in China, and he met with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. These are very important talks. We know that the war in Ukraine was not on the agenda. However, it is inevitable that what happens in China these next few days, all of the bilateral talks will have some significant impact. At the same time, there have been significant updates on the ground within Ukraine. To make sense of it all and tell us about these updates within Ukraine, we are joined by Peter Cororov, an independent journalist who is the author of the Substack “Events in Ukraine,” an incredible blog which I hope you all bookmark and subscribe to. Peter, thank you so much and welcome to the show. [Peter Cororov:] Thanks so much for having me. I’m really excited to talk about today. Well, you’ve been following what’s been happening in Ukraine very closely. Before we get into some of the more granular details of these different corruption schemes, foreign mercenaries, etc., I just want to give our viewers a brief overview of the battlefield situation right now. In this moment, could we say that either side has a strategic advantage? And what is the general sentiment that you’re perceiving with regards to peace talks at the moment? [Host:] This year has been interesting on the battlefield because Ukraine has mounted a number of different offensive operations. This has obviously gotten a lot of attention in the western press. It’s important for Ukraine to show that it still has these offensive capacities. But the big question is, of course, what results that gets and also how much Ukraine’s demographic capacities can really handle these offensive operations, which obviously result in plenty of casualties as the war does in general. The offensives haven’t really led to any significant results. There’s lots of debate over which sort of farmland area is under control of Ukraine or Russia, but Ukraine hasn’t managed to take any significant towns. So it’s kind of fighting over this farmland area with little strategic importance. Russia has moved forward slightly in some places. It’s taken most of these two relatively large towns, Toilia and Constant, but it hasn’t been a huge year of military victories on either side. Both governments consider themselves able to weather it out for a significant time longer. The Ukrainians have the Europeans funding them significant amounts. I think the Europeans just passed another 45 billion euros recently. So I don’t really have very high hopes for the negotiations, honestly. Ultimately, the demands on either side are still incommensurable. There’s not much chance, I don’t think. I think it’s mainly Trump has some kind of interest, largely domestic political interest, but I don’t think he really has the real willpower to force Ukraine to accept Russian demands. Even if he did, the Europeans are still there to continue aiding the Ukrainian military. That’s how I see it essentially at the moment. [Peter Cororov:] I don’t know if you saw earlier this morning, Hillary Clinton penned a wild opinion piece essentially criticizing Trump for having met with Vladimir Putin in China and saying, “This is what I would have said to Vladimir Putin if I was there.” Completely out of touch. She’s allegedly a top Democrat and somehow her main focus is why we’re not going to war on the side of Ukraine. Pretty crazy stuff there. But a very interesting element of the war has been the international character that the Ukrainian side has taken on. Beyond the amount of funding from European allies and the United States, the weapons, the political and diplomatic backing, we’re also talking about tens of thousands of foreign mercenaries fighting on behalf of Ukraine. Recently, reports have revealed that members of Mexican drug cartels, Colombian paramilitary groups, etc., are actually on the ground in Ukraine. You wrote about this in a recent piece on Substack called “Narotist.” You highlighted that of all the drone attacks in Latin America since 2018, 72% took place in 2025. This is very astounding. You argue that US support to Ukraine in its war with Russia in terms of intelligence training, weapons supply, etc., is not just about fighting Russia but is also about the US war on the global south. Explain this argument to our viewers. How is it that so many mercenaries, cartel members, and gang members are in Ukraine, and what role does the battlefield in Ukraine play vis-à-vis Washington’s agenda in the global south right now? [Host:] It’s a very interesting story. When I was researching that article, just recently this week, there’s a really remarkable story out of Brazil. I think the Brazilian story kind of encapsulates my broader argument about this and the broader tendencies you can see in Latin America. The majority of the Latin American volunteers are from Colombia. The latest Ukrainian estimates are 7,000 Colombians fighting for Ukraine, a total of 16,000 foreign volunteers. Then, a few thousand different Ecuadorians, Mexicans, and plenty of Brazilians. The Brazil story is very interesting. Basically, on the 12th of November, the Brazilian press reported on the arrest in Rio of a certain individual with the street name Predator. He’s a 26-year-old who spent five months fighting in Ukraine. He is a member of the Tercero Commando Puro (TCP) cartel. He was arrested for being a member of this cartel and was in charge of the security apparatus. It’s very interesting if you look at the actual nature of this cartel. TCP is the third largest cartel in Brazil. It’s actually a Pentecostal cartel. This is the phenomenon of narco-Pentecostalism in Brazil, where Pentecostalism, of American origin, is very right-wing, very opposed to Lula, and very aligned with the Bolsonaro movement. They are very pro-American, obviously. Cartels, as a business group that thrives off of exploiting the poor, have some sort of organic relationship or tendency for them to be interested in ideas of Pentecostalism and the idea that the state shouldn’t exist. This cartel, for instance, considers the state to be like Satan, and they need to fight against it. They are also very pro-Israel. They have a huge Star of David hanging in the neighborhoods they control in Rio, and they have flags of Israel everywhere. They are quite friendly with the police as far as cartels go, which is interesting considering the general right-wing tendency of police forces in Latin America. It’s very interesting that of all the cartels, the one that has been at least arrested for going to Ukraine is in this cartel. I think you can make the argument really if you look at the broader function of the cartels in Latin America. For instance, in Ecuador in 2024, there was this supposed cartel uprising. The right-wing president of Ecuador used this very well to declare a state of war and invited more US military presence within the country. It’s kind of a playbook all around Latin America. El Salvador is a similar case. Mexico still has a left-wing government, and there was also this strange case at the beginning of this year with an almost cartel uprising when the Mexican government assassinated or captured El Mencho, the head of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). There was an uprising against the government. The American right-wing press was amplifying this, trying to portray Mexico’s government as collapsing. Laura Loomer said that Sheinbaum had been evacuated, and the press secretary of the White House said military action is necessary if American citizens are threatened. Very much an attempt to use cartel instability as an excuse for US military intervention into this left-wing government, which Trump is not very happy with, and in general, most US administrations are not very happy with. The reason I bring up the name of the cartel is because there was a famous video in October from Al Jazeera on the topic of Latin American foreign fighters in Ukraine. There were about ten Latin Americans, and they said they had come back from missions in Ecuador, Colombia, and Mexico. At least one of them introduced himself as being from the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, which is quite striking. You can really see an interesting tendency. In terms of the way that these Latin Americans serve in the Ukrainian army, it’s often very close to the Ukrainian military intelligence apparatus. They serve in all units of the Ukrainian army, but they often tend to have special units just for them for language purposes. One particularly interesting example is a unit called the Advanced Company Unit, which has about 100-150 members. It’s part of Ukrainian military intelligence (GUR), which is the Ukrainian intelligence agency trained most by the CIA and MI6. There’s plenty in the western press about it. This unit, Advanced Company Unit, is led by a Brazilian gentleman named Le Anderson Paulino. He has a large Instagram profile and tries to accentuate how criminal he looks. There was a scandal at the start of this year where he beat one of his subordinates to death, with systematic torture and sexual abuse of recruits in this unit. It was covered by the Ukrainian western-funded press. You look at the members of this unit, and they look fairly unsavory. There’s probably strong evidence that this fellow in the Pentecostal cartel might have served in this unit because this is essentially a unit of Brazilian mercenaries in Ukraine. The Brazilian press talks about how it was some sort of military intelligence training unit. The GUR Ukrainian military intelligence, where this unit of Brazilian fighters is, is renowned for having their operators around the world. For instance, in the Sahel, training separatists. In September, the former head of the GUR, Budanov, who’s now Zelensky’s chief of staff, posted photographs of GUR operatives in Mali, which was quite something because until then, the Ukrainian foreign ministry had always denied any involvement. He proudly posted these photographs in Mali training Tuareg fighters. CNN has also written about it, how the Ukrainians have systematically trained them in the use of drones as drone operators. There’s a remarkable article I’m going to write about this week in the Ukrainian press, which claimed that Ukraine’s GUR operatives in Sudan were on the side of rebels fighting against General Al-Burhan, who is pro-Russian, which would mean the RSF, obviously, which is a remarkable statement to make. All that is said is that these GUR operatives have this existing tendency towards training US-aligned forces around the world. There are some cases in Congo, possibly to do with Rwanda. The final thing I would say is that there’s a recent book by Wall Street Journal correspondent Bojan Pancevski. He’s a pro-journalist. It’s about Nord Stream, but that’s not important. It has an interesting section in it when it talks about a 2017 training course that took place in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and in the US. It was curated by the CIA and Dutch intelligence, and then in the US, obviously just the CIA. It was for Ukrainian intelligence operatives to conduct covert work in foreign countries. According to Pancevski, who’s very pro-Ukrainian and pro-NATO, the aim was for them to be used in contexts conducive to US interests. He gave the example of Cuba and Mexico, which is quite interesting. There’s no evidence of any Ukrainian citizens or operatives in Latin America. But it is interesting that you have these cartel members from Latin America fighting in these Ukrainian intelligence agency units, getting drone training, and going back and then using this drone training in ways that are arguably fairly conducive to US foreign policy goals. [Peter Cororov:] It’s really harrowing, especially when you see the front lines of the anti-imperialist struggle being in the Sahel. This new imperialist onslaught against Latin America and this connection with Ukraine is quite concerning. I did want you to just dig in a bit more to the frequency of these drone strikes happening in 2025. Essentially, people are going to Ukraine, learning how to use these drones, and coming back. Where is this happening? You also wrote about Sergey Kurotikk, an influential figure in the Azov movement in the Ukrainian army. You said he is a follower of Santa Muerte and was even in Ecuador where he found these ideas. To add to this narrative, who is this figure and how are people like him playing a role in the recruitment of these far-right mercenaries? What does it say about the ideological character of this battlefield and the fight against Russia? [Host:] There’s an interesting statistic that last year alone, there were 34,000 drone flights detected by US law enforcement on the border with Mexico. The Mexican side even had a case recently where American law enforcement used a laser system to shoot down three drones near Texas, apparently controlled by Mexican cartels. There have been numerous cases as well. In October, there was a drone attack on the state attorney’s general’s office in Tijuana by cartels. They attacked the kidnapping units. There was also a raid in Sinaloa where they found 15 FPV drones and different specialized equipment. In Brazil, late last year, an anti-drone system that jams and shoots them down was discovered in a raid on a Brazilian cartel. The drone system had a Ukrainian nationalist trident on it, and it was written in English. The Brazilian press reported on it and got the opinion of some Ukrainian expert who said it might not be Ukrainian. The American expert community, like the CSIS based in Washington, has been writing about how cartels have used drones for a long time, long before the Ukraine war. But what’s difficult is actually operating the drones. It’s quite difficult to learn how to operate these drones, and the skills acquired on the battlefield in Ukraine are very useful. This is why Ukrainian drone operators have been going across the world to the Gulf to help the UAE and whatnot. It’s easy to buy drones, but actually having the skills to operate them is very different. Without training, you’re likely to fail navigating complex environments. There is definitely a strategy on the side of organized crime to send their operatives there. Ideologically, the majority of Colombians who go, it’s about 7,000 apparently fighting, is the largest Latin American group. They’re largely veterans of the armed forces or different other law enforcement units. Often in coverage of this, there’s a somewhat depoliticized view of it. They’re going for salary, which I’m sure is true to some extent as well. There’s an article by Ukrainian state media mentioning how the Colombians are fighting in Ukraine for the cause of freedom, but it also mentions how their experience fighting against guerillas back in Colombia has been very helpful for them. This is an interesting admission because the Colombian army law enforcement was forged fighting against left-wing guerrillas against FARC and so on, and also engaged in various massacres of peasant communities and often aligned with different right-wing paramilitaries that are essentially drug cartels. There are definitely ideological reasons why they might go to Ukraine, which also has this pervasive right-wing ideology, anti-communism. There’s an interesting Azov Ukrainian nationalist telegram channel with about 20,000 followers called Tales of the Fourth Empire. In 2019, there’s an interesting post where it talks about the campaign of murders of former FARC members in Colombia, and the author was very happy about this. He said that Ukraine should use a similar approach if we have a political settlement with the East Ukrainian pro-Russian separatists. They see it as a similar fight because anti-communism, anti-left-wing ideology is the main ideology of Azov. It makes sense why they would be aligned in that sense. There are obviously some Colombians that have gone to fight on the Russian side, but according to the estimates by the Ukrainians, it’s significantly less, about half less for the Russians than for the Ukrainians. There are all kinds. The last thing about Kurotikk, he’s a very interesting figure. There are rumors that before he was actually of Russian descent, but he was the second most important figure in the Azov movement from its founding until 2022. He’s sort of in the shadows now, but he’s very influential in the assault units, which are very famous and brutal units that have had many scandals in Ukrainian press because of systematic torture and execution of deserters. Kurotikk was one of the leaders of this group of units, which has about 20-30,000 troops in it. It still exists, although it’s been somewhat reformed supposedly. In 2019-2020, he said that he’s a big fan of Santa Muerte, which is a semi-religion of certain Latin American organized crime groups. It’s somewhat of a religion of death, some sort of satanic or something. He’s into it, and different satanic pagan beliefs are very popular in the post-Soviet white nationalist scene. He’s definitely an important figure in recruiting for these different units. He’s still very close to the assault units, and the assault units are actually very closely aligned with this Brazilian cartel group that I mentioned recently, the Advanced Company Unit. It’s part of this larger unit called Revenge, which is obviously a right-wing name, and they’re very right-wing. They’re neo-Nazis. You look in the telegram channels, and they’re always posting all this kind of stuff. They made a collection called the Christian Core two months ago, a collection of different units, and you have people from the assault units who come with organized crime background who are part of this collection and advertise themselves as being right-wing Christian nationalists. There’s a figure there, Kachinsky, who famously said that he wants there to be a Christian Taliban in Ukraine. He’s a bit of a comical figure, but also he’s in charge of a military unit, and he’s always calling to kill deserters on TV. There’s an ecosystem of these very right-wing figures in the Ukrainian army, many with organized crime links. Kurotikk, this Santa Muerte guy, is renowned for being an organized criminal. In the 2000s, when he was in Russia, he was part of a big murderous neo-Nazi group that killed dozens of migrants. He somehow escaped, but it was found that his bank account had 200 million rubles. He’s a very strange individual in Ukraine. He has a plane for some reason, a private plane. These are all figures that clearly have international connections, organized crime connections, and quite high-level positions in Europe’s largest army now. [Peter Cororov:] I know we’re going on here, but I do want to get your perspective on a couple more things. A couple of weeks ago, there was a lot of news about a secret detention center that was allegedly discovered. There were draft dodgers and deserters tortured and beaten. But then there was a strong pushback from mainstream media and Ukrainian politicians that this was all fabricated and somehow a Russian plot. Your thoughts on this? What really happened here? Beyond this specific media incident, what is the situation with regards to deserters and the general sentiment towards service right now? [Host:] There was an interesting video by a medic from the Azov. It was from the third corps, but basically the major Azov military unit. She complained on television that she went to a school and saw that school children don’t know anything about NATO. They don’t care about NATO, but they care a lot about these abuses by the mobilization forces called the TRC, territorial recruitment centers, which have become massively hated in Ukrainian society. She was very sad about this. She says there needs to be a re-education of the youth. Apparently, they don’t know anything about Azov’s main military operations. That’s just an example of how distant the nationalist elite is from the people, the majority of people that really don’t care about this massively bloody war, but they do care about when their relatives are dragged off the street, kicking and screaming, and sent into a bus, and they die within a few weeks. With this case in a suburb of Kiev, the whole media response of denying anything bad happened is quite funny because if you look at the Ukrainian press, every day there’s a new case of torture, extortion, deaths in the Ukrainian army, in the mobilization structures, the TRC. These are not reports by random people. These are criminal cases launched by Ukraine’s law enforcement agencies against individual representatives of the TRC. It’s totally systematic. There was a remarkable estimate by one Ukrainian MP that the amount of bribes each year is two billion euros. It’s huge in terms of getting out of the mobilization process. At every single step of the way, there’s someone you can pay a bribe to, and if you don’t pay the bribe, you get beaten. Ultimately, you’ll get sent to the front where you will likely die. There are endless schemes of how to pay this money, who to pay, huge business. Beatings are an essential part of it because it makes you more likely to pay. It’s also a way to discipline soldiers because these are civilians, they don’t really want to fight, and they need to be somehow disciplined into going into a battle where they will likely die. The point being is that this claim that nothing happened there, maybe there were some aspects because it became a very viral event in Kiev where many people got very excited and angry, and some of them had relatives stuck in there. There might have been some exaggerations. There was some report someone died there, we don’t know, but the thing is we don’t know. Maybe someone did die, but then last week, a week after this event, the military ombudsman, Ukraine’s military ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said that there probably were beatings in this place. The head of Ukraine’s chief of staff, Budanov, said when he went there to save the people from there that there are thousands of sites like this. This site was a temporary holding site where they keep soldiers that have violated discipline in some way. Some of them tried to desert, some of them may have been caught drinking or whatnot. Maybe some of them didn’t pay extortion fees, which are very common in the Ukrainian army as well, and they were kept there. We know from the photos that some of them were beaten. They had black eyes. The medical reports showed that there was one person there who had a stoma, so he had his stomach open. He basically went to the toilet through this tube and was just left there in this hole in the ground. He was getting an infection, disgusting abscess, and so on. These were terrible conditions. In the weeks since, there’s been no real investigation of the military. This was a military, it was Azov, it was the first national guard corps and first Azov corps, and they were the ones in charge of this place. There’s been no investigation into them, but there have been about 20 people arrested, protesters who protested outside of this building. They’ve been arrested and face 5 to 8 years in jail, very serious sentences for obstructing military personnel. These were just ordinary people, mainly young people. They were sent to jail for two months without any possibility of bail, which is quite a big contrast to these huge corruption cases in Ukraine where the ministers and people in Zelensky’s orbit sometimes get charged but with the possibility of bail, so they just pay the bail and leave quite early. This happens very regularly, whereas ordinary people obviously don’t have this option. There have been quite a few of these protests this year against mobilization. In June or July, there was a large protest in Lviv, which is a western city known for being very nationalist. People there are very angry about mobilization as well. There was a large protest of mainly youth against the mobilization authorities, and the police scared them away eventually. They managed to free some person from the mobilization, and then in the weeks later, the nationalists, Azov, captured these youth. They forced them to apologize on camera. One person had been visibly very severely beaten or tortured. He was crying and giving this apology, and he was going to be sent to the army. This is a video that was posted proudly by Azov people who call to kill all draft dodgers. They’re all cowards. The video is harrowing. The guy is an adult, in his mid-20s, looks like a guy from the streets, not a sensitive guy, and he’s barely able to say anything. Something really terrible was done to him. That’s what happens. [Peter Cororov:] Really harrowing stuff. One last thing I wanted to hear from you about is this corruption scandal in Ukraine with regards to the Himrom cartel and its dealings in drug trafficking and call center mafia. Briefly give us an overview of what’s happening with this scandal. What role does this cartel play in Ukrainian politics? What does it say about the Zelensky government and this so-called defense of freedom and democracy that Europe and the Democratic Party in the US are so eager to join and support? [Host:] This is a pretty remarkable story. On a diplomatic level, this organized crime group called Himrom, its leader currently lives in Mexico. It’s just one group of scam call centers. It controlled about 50 scam call centers. There was a peak of about 1,500 scam call centers. In total, these scam call centers, according to European Swiss organized crime investigators, generated 12 billion dollars a year, which is huge numbers. 85% of their victims were not Russian but European. The propaganda line in Ukraine always was these scam call centers are fine because they only scam Russian grandmothers, which often causes suicides. These are very sadistic people. They have TikToks, and they talk about it, very proud of it, and share their funniest stories of when some pensioner said they’re going to commit suicide or whatever because they scammed them out of everything, and they revel in this. Even the scam call center cartel person said that probably the scam call centers are evil because of the damage done to the employees, the psychological damage. According to the Swiss press, they employed about 100,000 people, which is remarkable, a huge amount of people. There are very few jobs in Ukraine nowadays. You’ll often see advertisements for these scam call centers. The Russian government managed to crack down on them fairly well, and now for the past few years, they’ve really been targeting Europeans. According to this head of Himrom, there’s even specialized scam call centers that target only America, only the United States. According to him, the head of Himrom, he says that the scam call centers generated $20 billion a year for Ukraine, not 12 billion like the Swiss, which is entirely possible. Ukrainian law enforcement, this is the European-funded section of Ukrainian law enforcement, released transcripts of wiretap conversations showing the head of Himrom talking with top figures in Ukraine’s intelligence agencies, law enforcement agencies about the rent they would get. Burkin said, “Yes, it’s all true.” Each scam call center would pay $21,000 US each month to the big three law enforcement agencies: the security services, the national police, and the general prosecutor. Last month, Ukraine’s general prosecutor, technically the most powerful law enforcement figure in the country, fled to Austria because of this whole investigation into his curation of these scam call centers and his profiting off these scam call centers. This is a figure close with Zelensky, known for being very loyal to Zelensky. The same is true for the National Police and Services. They’ve all been identified as being involved with these scam call centers. If you add up the number of bribes they were getting, the Himrom leader says it added up to $370 million US a year just in bribes to the Ukrainian government to keep these scam call centers open. If you don’t pay the bribes, they would raid the scam call center, close it down, and so on. The last interesting thing about this is that there’s been nothing in the western press about this. Before last year, Zelensky tried to close down the anti-corruption agencies that the western countries had set up to control the Ukrainian government in a sense. When Zelensky tried to shut them down, there was lots in the western press about Zelensky abandoning democracy. It’s very bad. Zelensky backed down and let them be. These anti-corruption agencies are very pro-NATO, very supportive of continuing the war. But now there’s nothing about this huge scandal of the Ukrainian government curating scams targeting European citizens in the European press. This is information revealed by law enforcement agencies that Europe created and sponsors and protects. It’s not a Russian psy-op or whatever. I think it’s because there are negotiations right now. The Europeans don’t want to damage Zelensky’s position. They want him to continue the war. If they damage his image, there could be more dissent in Europe about whether this is a government that should be supported with billions of dollars. The fact that the European press hasn’t covered it at all is a testament to this. This is also why I don’t really believe that much in these negotiations, unfortunately, because the Europeans seem very intent on the Ukraine project. [Peter Cororov:] Yeah, and as if it weren’t costing billions of dollars and more importantly tens of thousands of lives. Peter, thank you so much for joining us and really digging into all of these different elements. I know it was a lot, but there’s just so much to discuss. You are the only person who can read not only the Ukrainian press and tell us what’s happening on the ground but provide excellent analysis. Thank you so much for joining us here at BT Live. [Peter Cororov:] Thanks so much.
